The younger son of Jacob by Rachel ([Gen. 35:18](#Gen.35.18)). His birth took place at Ephrath, on the road between Bethel and Bethlehem, at a short distance from the latter place. His mother died in giving him birth, and with her last breath named him Ben-oni, son of my pain, a name which was changed by his father into Benjamin. His posterity are called Benjamites ([Gen. 49:27](#Gen.49.27); [Deut. 33:12](#Deut.33.12); [Josh. 18:21](#Josh.18.21)).
The father of Balaam ([Num. 22:5](#Num.22.5); [24:3](#Num.24.3), [15](#Num.24.15); [31:8](#Num.31.8)). In 2 Pet. 2:15 he is called Bosor.
The father of Bela, one of the kings of Edom ([Gen. 36:32](#Gen.36.32)).
Gift, or son of evil, king of Sodom at the time of the invasion of the four kings under Chedorlaomer ([Gen. 14:2](#Gen.14.2), [8](#Gen.14.8), [17](#Gen.14.17), [21](#Gen.14.21)).
One of the Benjamite warriors, Saul’s brethren, who joined David when at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:3](#1Chr.12.3)).
Son of Shimea, and father of Asaph the musician ([1 Chr. 6:39](#1Chr.6.39); [15:17](#1Chr.15.17)).
The fourth of the five sons of Zerubbabel, of the royal family of Judah ([1 Chr. 3:20](#1Chr.3.20)).
One of the seven Ephraimite chieftains, son of Meshillemoth ([2 Chr. 28:12](#2Chr.28.12)).
A son of Shuthelah, and grandson of Ephraim ([1 Chr. 7:20](#1Chr.7.20)).
One of Asher’s four sons, and father of Heber ([Gen. 46:17](#Gen.46.17)).
A Benjamite who with his brother Shema founded Ajalon and expelled the Gittites ([1 Chr. 8:13](#1Chr.8.13)).
A son of Ephraim ([1 Chr. 7:20-23](#1Chr.7.20)), born after the slaughter of his brothers, and so called by his father “because it went evil with his house” at that time.

Bearer of victory, the eldest daughter of Agrippa I., the Herod Agrippa of [Acts 12:20](#Acts.12.20). After the early death of her first husband she was married to her uncle Herod, king of Chalcis. After his death (A.D. 40) she lived in incestuous connection with her brother Agrippa II. ([Acts 25:13](#Acts.25.13), [23](#Acts.25.23); 26:30). They joined the Romans at the outbreak of the final war between them and the Jews, and lived afterwards at Rome.

The son of Nahor by Milcah; nephew of Abraham, and father of Rebekah ([Gen. 22:22](#Gen.22.22), [23](#Gen.22.23); [24:15](#Gen.24.15), [24](#Gen.24.24), [47](#Gen.24.47)). He appears in person only once (24:50).

In the shadow of God; i.e., “under his protection”, the artificer who executed the work of art in connection with the tabernacle in the wilderness ([Ex. 31:2](#Exod.31.2); [35:30](#Exod.35.30)). He was engaged principally in works of metal, wood, and stone; while Aholiab, who was associated with him and subordinate to him, had the charge of the textile fabrics (36:1, 2; 38:22). He was of the tribe of Judah, the son of Uri, and grandson of Hur (31:2). Mention is made in [Ezra 10:30](#Ezra.10.30) of another of the same name.
Garden, or gift of fortune, one of the seven eunuchs or chamberlains who had charge of the harem of Ahasuerus ([Esther 1:10](#Esth.1.10)).

One of the eunuchs who “kept the door” in the court of Ahasuerus. With Teresh he conspired against the king’s life. Mordecai detected the conspiracy, and the culprits were hanged ([Esther 2:21-23](#Esth.2.21); [6:1-3](#Esth.6.1)).

Son of contention, one of Job’s friends. He is called “the Shuhite,” probably as belonging to Shuah, a district in Arabia, in which Shuah, the sixth son of Abraham by Keturah, settled ([Gen. 25:2](#Gen.25.2)). He took part in each of the three controversies into which Job’s friends entered with him ([Job 8:1](#Job.8.1); [18:1](#Job.18.1); [25:1](#Job.25.1)), and delivered three speeches, very severe and stern in their tone, although less violent than those of Zophar, but more so than those of Eliphaz.
A priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel ([Neh. 12:5](#Neh.12.5), [18](#Neh.12.18)).
The head of the fifteenth sacerdotal course for the temple service ([1 Chr. 24:14](#1Chr.24.14)).

Faltering; bashful, Rachel’s handmaid, whom she gave to Jacob ([Gen. 29:29](#Gen.29.29)). She was the mother of Dan and Naphtali ([Gen. 30:3-8](#Gen.30.3)). Reuben was cursed by his father for committing adultry with her (35:22; 49:4). He was deprived of the birth-right, which was given to the sons of Joseph.
Son of the tongue; i.e., “eloquent”, a man of some note who returned from the Captivity with Zerubbabel ([Ezra 2:2](#Ezra.2.2); [Neh. 7:7](#Neh.7.7)).
Son of wickedness, a king of Gomorrah whom Abraham succoured in the invasion of Chedorlaomer ([Gen. 14:2](#Gen.14.2)).
Chamberlain to king Herod Agrippa I. ([Acts 12:20](#Acts.12.20)). Such persons generally had great influence with their masters.
The husband of Ruth, a wealthy Bethlehemite. By the “levirate law” the duty devolved on him of marrying Ruth the Moabitess ([Ruth 4:1-13](#Ruth.4.1)). He was a kinsman of Mahlon, her first husband.
The second son of Nahor and Milcah, and brother of Huz ([Gen. 22:21](#Gen.22.21)). Elihu was one of his descendants ([Job 32:2](#Job.32.2)).
One of the chiefs of the tribe of Gad ([1 Chr. 5:14](#1Chr.5.14)).

The Jewish high priest (A.D. 27-36) at the beginning of our Lord’s public ministry, in the reign of Tiberius ([Luke 3:2](#Luke.3.2)), and also at the time of his condemnation and crucifixion ([Matt. 26:3](#Matt.26.3), [57](#Matt.26.57); [John 11:49](#John.11.49); [18:13](#John.18.13), [14](#John.18.14)). He held this office during the whole of Pilate’s administration. His wife was the daughter of Annas, who had formerly been high priest, and was probably the vicar or deputy (Heb. sagan) of Caiaphas. …

The first-born son of Adam and Eve ([Gen. 4](#Gen.4)). He became a tiller of the ground, as his brother Abel followed the pursuits of pastoral life. He was “a sullen, self-willed, haughty, vindictive man; wanting the religious element in his character, and defiant even in his attitude towards God.” It came to pass “in process of time” (marg. “at the end of days”), i.e., probably on the Sabbath, that the two brothers presented their offerings to the Lord. …

The fourth antediluvian patriarch, the eldest son of Enos. He was 70 years old at the birth of his eldest son Mahalaleel, after which he lived 840 years ([Gen. 5:9-14](#Gen.5.9)), and was 910 years old when he died. He is also called Kenan ([1 Chr. 1:2](#1Chr.1.2)).
The son of Arphaxad ([Luke 3:36](#Luke.3.36)). He is nowhere named in the Old Testament. He is usually called the “second Cainan.”
([1 Chr. 2:6](#1Chr.2.6)), sustenance, the same probably as Chalcol ([1 Kings 4:31](#1Kgs.4.31)), one of the four sages whom Solomon excelled in wisdom; for “he was wiser than all men.”

The son of Jephunneh ([Num. 13:6](#Num.13.6); [32:12](#Num.32.12); [Josh. 14:6](#Josh.14.6), [14](#Josh.14.14)). He was one of those whom Moses sent to search the land in the second year after the Exodus. He was one of the family chiefs of the tribe of Judah. …
One of the three sons of Hezron of the tribe of Judah. He is also called Chelubai ([1 Chr. 2:9](#1Chr.2.9)). His descendants are enumerated (18-20, 42-49).

The fourth son of Ham ([Gen. 10:6](#Gen.10.6)). His descendants were under a curse in consequence of the transgression of his father (9:22-27). His eldest son, Zidon, was the father of the Sidonians and Phoenicians. He had eleven sons, who were the founders of as many tribes (10:15-18).

The queen of the Ethiopians whose “eunuch” or chamberlain was converted to Christianity by the instrumentality of Philip the evangelist ([Acts 8:27](#Acts.8.27)). The country which she ruled was called by the Greeks Meroe, in Upper Nubia. It was long the centre of commercial intercourse between Africa and the south of Asia, and hence became famous for its wealth ([Isa. 45:14](#Isa.45.14)).
The last named of the four sons of Reuben ([Gen. 46:9](#Gen.46.9)).
The son of Zimri, and the father of Achan ([Josh. 7:1](#Josh.7.1)), “the troubler of Israel.”

Fortified, a people descended from Mizraim ([Gen. 10:14](#Gen.10.14); [1 Chr. 1:12](#1Chr.1.12)). Their original seat was probably somewhere in Lower Egypt, along the sea-coast to the south border of Palestine.

(= Khudur-Lagamar of the inscriptions), king of Elam. Many centuries before the age of Abraham, Canaan and even the Sinaitic peninsula had been conquered by Babylonian kings, and in the time of Abraham himself Babylonia was ruled by a dynasty which claimed sovereignity over Syria and Palestine. The kings of the dynasty bore names which were not Babylonian, but at once South Arabic and Hebrew. The most famous king of the dynasty was Khammu-rabi, who united Babylonia under one rule, and made Babylon its capital. …

The destroyer, subduer, or fish-god, the god of the Moabites ([Num. 21:29](#Num.21.29); [Jer. 48:7](#Jer.48.7), [13](#Jer.48.13), [46](#Jer.48.46)). The worship of this god, “the abomination of Moab,” was introduced at Jerusalem by Solomon ([1 Kings 11:7](#1Kgs.11.7)), but was abolished by Josiah ([2 Kings 23:13](#2Kgs.23.13)). On the “Moabite Stone” (q.v.), Mesha ([2 Kings 3:5](#2Kgs.3.5)) ascribes his victories over the king of Israel to this god, “And Chemosh drove him before my sight.”
Whom Jehovah hath made. “Chief of the Levites,” probably a Kohathite ([1 Chr. 15:22](#1Chr.15.22)), and therefore not the same as mentioned in 26:29.
The pining one, the younger son of Elimelech and Naomi, and husband of Orpah, Ruth’s sister ([Ruth 1:2](#Ruth.1.2); [4:9](#Ruth.4.9)).
Verdure, a female Christian ([1 Cor. 1:11](#1Cor.1.11)), some of whose household had informed Paul of the divided state of the Corinthian church. Nothing is known of her.

Cush of double wickedness, or governor of two presidencies, the king of Mesopotamia who oppressed Israel in the generation immediately following Joshua ([Judg. 3:8](#Judg.3.8)). We learn from the Tell-el-Amarna tablets that Palestine had been invaded by the forces of Aram-naharaim (A.V., “Mesopotamia”) more than once, long before the Exodus, and that at the time they were written the king of Aram-naharaim was still intriguing in Canaan. …

A female Christian mentioned in [2 Tim. 4:21](#2Tim.4.21). It is a conjecture having some probability that she was a British maiden, the daughter of king Cogidunus, who was an ally of Rome, and assumed the name of the emperor, his patron, Tiberius Claudius, and that she was the wife of Pudens.

The fourth Roman emperor. He succeeded Caligula (A.D. 41). Though in general he treated the Jews, especially those in Asia and Egypt, with great indulgence, yet about the middle of his reign (A.D. 49) he banished them all from Rome ([Acts 18:2](#Acts.18.2)). In this edict the Christians were included, as being, as was supposed, a sect of Jews. The Jews, however soon again returned to Rome.
Claudius Lysias, a Greek who, having obtained by purchase the privilege of Roman citizenship, took the name of Claudius ([Acts 21:31-40](#Acts.21.31); [22:28](#Acts.22.28); [23:26](#Acts.23.26)).

Mild, a Christian of Philippi, Paul’s “fellow-labourer,” whose name he mentions as “in the book of life” ([Phil. 4:3](#Phil.4.3)). It was an opinion of ancient writers that he was the Clement of Rome whose name is well known in church history, and that he was the author of an Epistle to the Corinthians, the only known manuscript of which is appended to the Alexandrian Codex, now in the British Museum. It is of some historical interest, and has given rise to much discussion among critics. It makes distinct reference to Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians.

(abbreviation of Cleopatros), one of the two disciples with whom Jesus conversed on the way to Emmaus on the day of the resurrection ([Luke 24:18](#Luke.24.18)). We know nothing definitely regarding him. It is not certain that he was the Clopas of [John 19:25](#John.19.25), or the Alphaeus of [Matt. 10:3](#Matt.10.3), although he may have been so.
Whom Jehovah hath set, a Levite placed over the tithes brought into the temple ([2 Chr. 35:9](#2Chr.35.9)).

A centurion whose history is narrated in [Acts 10](#Acts.10). He was a “devout man,” and like the centurion of Capernaum, believed in the God of Israel. His residence at Caesrea probably brought him into contact with Jews who communicated to him their expectations regarding the Messiah; and thus he was prepared to welcome the message Peter brought him. He became the first fruit of the Gentile world to Christ. He and his family were baptized and admitted into the Christian church ([Acts 10:1](#Acts.10.1), [44](#Acts.10.44)-48).
A descendant of Judah. [1 Chr. 4:8](#1Chr.4.8), “Coz;” R.V., “Hakkoz.”
Increasing, probably one of the seventy disciples of Christ. He was one of Paul’s assistants ([2 Tim. 4:10](#2Tim.4.10)), probably a Christian of Rome.
Curled, the chief of the synagogue at Corinth ([Acts 18:8](#Acts.18.8)). He was converted and, with his family, baptized by Paul ([1 Cor. 1:14](#1Cor.1.14)).

A son, probably the eldest, of Ham, and the father of Nimrod ([Gen. 10:8](#Gen.10.8); [1 Chr. 1:10](#1Chr.1.10)). From him the land of Cush seems to have derived its name. The question of the precise locality of the land of Cush has given rise to not a little controversy. The second river of Paradise surrounded the whole land of Cush ([Gen. 2:13](#Gen.2.13), R.V.). The term Cush is in the Old Testament generally applied to the countries south of the Israelites. …

The Grecized form of Quirinus. His full name was Publius Sulpicius Quirinus. Recent historical investigation has proved that Quirinus was governor of Cilicia, which was annexed to Syria at the time of our Lord’s birth. Cilicia, which he ruled, being a province of Syria, he is called the governor, which he was de jure, of Syria. Some ten years afterwards he was appointed governor of Syria for the second time. During his tenure of office, at the time of our Lord’s birth ([Luke 2:2](#Luke.2.2)), a “taxing” (R.V., “enrolment;” i.e., a registration) of the people was “first made;” i.e., was made for the first time under his government.

(Heb. Ko’resh), the celebrated “King of Persia” (Elam) who was conqueror of Babylon, and issued the decree of liberation to the Jews ([Ezra 1:1](#Ezra.1.1), [2](#Ezra.1.2)). He was the son of Cambyses, the prince of Persia, and was born about B.C. 599. In the year B.C. 559 he became king of Persia, the kingdom of Media being added to it partly by conquest. Cyrus was a great military leader, bent on universal conquest. Babylon fell before his army (B.C. 538) on the night of Belshazzar’s feast ([Dan. 5:30](#Dan.5.30)), and then the ancient dominion of Assyria was also added to his empire (cf., “Go up, O Elam”, [Isa. 21:2](#Isa.21.2)).

Little fish; diminutive from dag = a fish, the fish-god; the national god of the Philistines ([Judg. 16:23](#Judg.16.23)). This idol had the body of a fish with the head and hands of a man. It was an Assyrio-Babylonian deity, the worship of which was introduced among the Philistines through Chaldea. The most famous of the temples of Dagon were at Gaza ([Judg. 16:23-30](#Judg.16.23)) and Ashdod ([1 Sam. 5:1-7](#1Sam.5.1)).
A heifer, an Athenian woman converted to Christianity under the preaching of Paul ([Acts 17:34](#Acts.17.34)). Some have supposed that she may have been the wife of Dionysius the Areopagite.

The fifth son of Jacob. His mother was Bilhah, Rachel’s maid ([Gen. 30:6](#Gen.30.6), “God hath judged me”, Heb. dananni). The blessing pronounced on him by his father was, “Dan shall judge his people” (49:16), probably in allusion to the judgeship of Samson, who was of the tribe of Dan.
Beltis protect the king!, the Chaldee name given to Daniel by Nebuchadnezzar ([Dan. 1:7](#Dan.1.7)).
David’s second son, “born unto him in Hebron, of Abigail the Carmelitess” ([1 Chr. 3:1](#1Chr.3.1)). He is called also Chileab ([2 Sam. 3:3](#2Sam.3.3)).
Pearl of wisdom, one of the four who were noted for their wisdom, but whom Solomon excelled ([1 Kings 4:31](#1Kgs.4.31)).

Darius the Persian ([Neh. 12:22](#Neh.12.22)) was probably the Darius II. (Ochus or Nothus) of profane history, the son of Artaxerxes Longimanus, who was the son and successor of Ahasuerus (Xerxes). There are some, however, who think that the king here meant was Darius III. (Codomannus), the antagonist of Alexander the Great (B.C. 336-331).

Welled; belonging to a fountain, a son of Eliab, a Reubenite, who joined Korah (q.v.) in his conspiracy, and with his accomplices was swallowed up by an earthquake ([Num. 16:1](#Num.16.1); [26:9](#Num.26.9); [Deut. 11:6](#Deut.11.6); [Ps. 106:17](#Ps.106.17)).

The princess who adopted the infant Moses (q.v.), [Ex. 2:10](#Exod.2.10). She is twice mentioned in the New Testament ([Acts 7:21](#Acts.7.21): [Heb. 11:24](#Heb.11.24)). It would seem that she was alive and in some position of influence about the court when Moses was compelled to flee from Egypt, and thus for forty years he had in some way been under her influence. She was in all probability the sister of Rameses, and the daughter of Seti I. Josephus calls her Thermuthis. It is supposed by some that she was Nefert-ari, the wife as well as sister of Rameses. The mummy of this queen was among the treasures found at Deir-el-Bahari.
The wife of Solomon ([1 Kings 3:1](#1Kgs.3.1)). This is the first reference since the Exodus to any connection of Israel with Egypt.

Beloved, the eighth and youngest son of Jesse, a citizen of Bethlehem. His father seems to have been a man in humble life. His mother’s name is not recorded. Some think she was the Nahash of [2 Sam. 17:25](#2Sam.17.25). As to his personal appearance, we only know that he was red-haired, with beautiful eyes and a fair face ([1 Sam. 16:12](#1Sam.16.12); [17:42](#1Sam.17.42)).

The king of Eglon, one of the five Canaanitish kings who were hanged by Joshua ([Josh. 10:3](#Josh.10.3), [23](#Josh.10.23)) after the victory at Gibeon. These kings fled and took refuge in a cave at Makkedah. Here they were kept confined till Joshua returned from the pursuit of their discomfited armies, when he caused them to be brought forth, and “Joshua smote them, and slew them, and hanged them on five trees” (26).

A prophetess, “wife” (woman?) of Lapidoth. Jabin, the king of Hazor, had for twenty years held Israel in degrading subjection. The spirit of patriotism seemed crushed out of the nation. In this emergency Deborah roused the people from their lethargy. Her fame spread far and wide. She became a “mother in Israel” ([Judg. 4:6](#Judg.4.6), [14](#Judg.4.14); 5:7), and “the children of Israel came up to her for judgment” as she sat in her tent under the palm tree “between Ramah and Bethel.” Preparations were everywhere made by her direction for the great effort to throw off the yoke of bondage. …

A son of Raamah ([Gen. 10:7](#Gen.10.7)). His descendants are mentioned in [Isa. 21:13](#Isa.21.13), and [Ezek. 27:15](#Ezek.27.15). They probably settled among the sons of Cush, on the north-west coast of the Persian Gulf.
A son of Jokshan, Abraham’s son by Keturah ([1 Chr. 1:32](#1Chr.1.32)). His descendants settled on the Syrian borders about the territory of Edom. They probably led a pastoral life.
The head of one of the bands of exiles that returned under Zerubbabel to Jerusalem ([Ezra 2:60](#Ezra.2.60); [Neh. 7:62](#Neh.7.62)).
A son of Shemaiah, and one of the courtiers to whom Jeremiah’s first roll of prophecy was read ([Jer. 36:12](#Jer.36.12)).
The head of the twenty-third division of the priestly order ([1 Chr. 24:18](#1Chr.24.18)).

Languishing, a Philistine woman who dwelt in the valley of Sorek ([Judg. 16:4-20](#Judg.16.4)). She was bribed by the “lords of the Philistines” to obtain from Samson the secret of his strength and the means of overcoming it ([Judg. 16:4-18](#Judg.16.4)). She tried on three occasions to obtain from him this secret in vain. On the fourth occasion she wrung it from him. She made him sleep upon her knees, and then called the man who was waiting to help her; who “cut off the seven locks of his head,” and so his “strength went from him.”

A companion and fellow-labourer of Paul during his first imprisonment at Rome ([Philemon 1](#Phlm.1.1):24; [Col. 4:14](#Col.4.14)). It appears, however, that the love of the world afterwards mastered him, and he deserted the apostle ([2 Tim. 4:10](#2Tim.4.10)).

A silversmith at Ephesus, whose chief occupation was to make “silver shrines for Diana” (q.v.), [Acts 19:24](#Acts.19.24), i.e., models either of the temple of Diana or of the statue of the goddess. This trade brought to him and his fellow-craftsmen “no small gain,” for these shrines found a ready sale among the countless thousands who came to this temple from all parts of Asia Minor. This traffic was greatly endangered by the progress of the gospel, and hence Demetrius excited the tradesmen employed in the manufacture of these shrines, and caused so great a tumult that “the whole city was filled with confusion.”

So called by the Romans; called Artemis by the Greeks, the “great” goddess worshipped among heathen nations under various modifications. Her most noted temple was that at Ephesus. It was built outside the city walls, and was one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. “First and last it was the work of 220 years; built of shining marble; 342 feet long by 164 feet broad; supported by a forest of columns, each 56 feet high; a sacred museum of masterpieces of sculpture and painting. …
Doubled cakes, the mother of Gomer, who was Hosea’s wife ([Hos. 1:3](#Hos.1.3)).

Judged; vindicated, daughter of Jacob by Leah, and sister of Simeon and Levi ([Gen. 30:21](#Gen.30.21)). She was seduced by Shechem, the son of Hamor, the Hivite chief, when Jacob’s camp was in the neighbourhood of Shechem. This led to the terrible revenge of Simeon and Levi in putting the Shechemites to death ([Gen. 34](#Gen.34)). Jacob makes frequent reference to this deed of blood with abhorrence and regret ([Gen. 34:30](#Gen.34.30); [49:5-7](#Gen.49.5)). She is mentioned among the rest of Jacob’s family that went down into Egypt ([Gen. 46:8](#Gen.46.8), [15](#Gen.46.15)).
The Areopagite, one of Paul’s converts at Athens ([Acts 17:34](#Acts.17.34)).
Antelope, the youngest son of Seir the Horite, head of one of the tribes of Idumaea ([Gen. 36:21](#Gen.36.21), [28](#Gen.36.28), [30](#Gen.36.30)).

Leaders, a race descended from Javan ([Gen. 10:4](#Gen.10.4)). They are known in profane history as the Dardani, originally inhabiting Illyricum. They were a semi-Pelasgic race, and in the ethnographical table ([Gen. 10](#Gen.10)) they are grouped with the Chittim (q.v.). In [1 Chr. 1:7](#1Chr.1.7), they are called Rodanim. The LXX. and the Samaritan Version also read Rhodii, whence some have concluded that the Rhodians, the inhabitants of the island of Rhodes, are meant.
An Ahohite, father of Eleazar, who was one of David’s three heroes ([2 Sam. 23:9](#2Sam.23.9); [1 Chr. 11:12](#1Chr.11.12)). He was the same with Dodai mentioned in [1 Chr. 27:4](#1Chr.27.4).
A Bethlehemite, and father of Elhanan, who was one of David’s thirty heroes ([2 Sam. 23:24](#2Sam.23.24)).

Fearful, an Edomite, the chief overseer of Saul’s flocks ([1 Sam. 21:7](#1Sam.21.7)). At the command of Saul he slew the high priest Ahimelech (q.v.) at Nob, together with all the priests to the number of eighty-five persons. (Comp. [Ps. 52](#Ps.52), title.)

(in Greek called Dorcas), gazelle, a disciple at Joppa. She was distinguished for her alms-deeds and good works. Peter, who was sent for from Lydda on the occasion of her death, prayed over the dead body, and said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes and sat up; and Peter “gave her his hand, and raised her up; and calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive” ([Acts 9:36-43](#Acts.9.36)).

Third and youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I. ([Acts 12:1-4](#Acts.12.1), [20-23](#Acts.12.20)). Felix, the Roman procurator of Judea, induced her to leave her husband, Azizus, the king of Emesa, and become his wife. She was present with Felix when Paul reasoned of “righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come” ([Acts 24:24](#Acts.24.24)). She and her son perished in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, A.D. 79.
A descendant of Seir the Horite ([Gen. 36:23](#Gen.36.23)).
A descendant of Eber ([1 Chr. 1:22](#1Chr.1.22)), called also Obal ([Gen. 10:28](#Gen.10.28)).
Slave, the father of Gaal, in whom the men of Shechem “put confidence” in their conspiracy against Abimelech ([Judg. 9:26](#Judg.9.26), [26](#Judg.9.26), [30](#Judg.9.30), [31](#Judg.9.31)).

The third post-duluvian patriach after Shem ([Gen. 10:24](#Gen.10.24); [11:14](#Gen.11.14)). He is regarded as the founder of the Hebrew race (10:21; [Num. 24:24](#Num.24.24)). In [Luke 3:35](#Luke.3.35) he is called Heber.
The oldest of the three sons of Elpaal the Benjamite ([1 Chr. 8:12](1chr/#1Chr.8.12)).
The head of the priestly family of Amok in the time of Zerubbabel ([Neh. 12:20](#Neh.12.20)).
Father of gathering; the gatherer, the youngest of the three sons of Korah the Levite, head of a family of Korhites ([Ex. 6:24](#Exod.6.24)); called Ebisaph ([1 Chr. 6:37](#1Chr.6.37)).
Son of Joah, and one of the Levites who assisted in reforming the public worship of the sanctuary in the time of Hezekiah ([2 Chr. 29:12](#2Chr.29.12)).
The second of the three sons of Mushi, of the family of Merari, appointed to the Levitical office ([1 Chr. 23:23](#1Chr.23.23); [24:30](#1Chr.24.30)).
A heifer, one of David’s wives, and mother of Ithream ([2 Sam. 3:5](#2Sam.3.5); [1 Chr. 3:3](#1Chr.3.3)). According to a Jewish tradition she was Michal.

Chieftain or king of one of the Moabite tribes ([Judg. 3:12-14](#Judg.3.12)). Having entered into an alliance with Ammon and Amalek, he overran the trans-Jordanic region, and then crossing the Jordan, seized on Jericho, the “city of palm trees,” which had been by this time rebuilt, but not as a fortress. He made this city his capital, and kept Israel in subjection for eighteen years. The people at length “cried unto the Lord” in their distress, and he “raised them up a deliverer” in Ehud (q.v.), the son of Gera, a Benjamite.

The son of Gera, of the tribe of Benjamin ([Judg. 3:15](#Judg.3.15)). After the death of Othniel the people again fell into idolatry, and Eglon, the king of Moab, uniting his bands with those of the Ammonites and the Amalekites, crossed the Jordan and took the city of Jericho, and for eighteen years held that whole district in subjection, exacting from it an annual tribute. At length Ehud, by a stratagem, put Eglon to death with a two-edged dagger a cubit long, and routed the Moabites at the fords of the Jordan, putting 10,000 of them to death. …
A descendant of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 7:10](#1Chr.7.10)), his great-grandson.

The son and successor of Baasha, king of Israel ([1 Kings 16:8-10](#1Kgs.16.8)). He was killed while drunk by Zimri, one of the captains of his chariots, and was the last king of the line of Baasha. Thus was fullfilled the prophecy of Jehu (6, 7, 11-14).
The father of Hoshea, the last king of Israel ([2 Kings 15:30](#2Kgs.15.30); [17:1](#2Kgs.17.1)).
One of the Edomite chiefs or “dukes” of Mount Seir ([Gen. 36:41](#Gen.36.41)).
The second of the three sons of Caleb, the son of Jephunneh ([1 Chr. 4:15](#1Chr.4.15)).

Highland, the son of Shem ([Gen. 10:22](#Gen.10.22)), and the name of the country inhabited by his descendants (14:1, 9; [Isa. 11:11](#Isa.11.11); [21:2](#Isa.21.2), etc.) lying to the east of Babylonia, and extending to the shore of the Mediterranean, a distance in a direct line of about 1,000 miles. The name Elam is an Assyrian word meaning “high.”
The son of Shaphan, one of the two who were sent by Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar, and also took charge of Jeremiah’s letter to the captives in Babylon ([Jer. 29:3](#Jer.29.3)).

Whom God has loved, one of the seventy elders whom Moses appointed ([Num. 11:26](#Num.11.26), [27](#Num.11.27)) to administer justice among the people. He, with Medad, prophesied in the camp instead of going with the rest to the tabernacle, as Moses had commanded. This incident was announced to Moses by Joshua, who thought their conduct in this respect irregular. Moses replied, “Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the Lord’s people were prophets” ([Num. 11:24-30](#Num.11.24); comp. [Mark 9:38](#Mark.9.38); [Luke 9:49](#Luke.9.49)).
A descendant of king Saul ([1 Chr. 8:37](#1Chr.8.37); [9:43](#1Chr.9.43)).
One of the descendants of Judah, of the family of Hezron ([1 Chr. 2:39](#1Chr.2.39), “Eleasah”).

The third son of Aaron ([Ex. 6:23](#Exod.6.23)). His wife, a daughter of Putiel, bore him Phinehas ([Ex. 6:25](#Exod.6.25)). After the death of Nadab and Abihu ([Lev. 10:12](#Lev.10.12); [Num. 3:4](#Num.3.4)) he was appointed to the charge of the sanctuary ([Num. 3:32](#Num.3.32)). On Mount Hor he was clothed with the sacred vestments, which Moses took from off his brother Aaron and put upon him as successor to his father in the high priest’s office, which he held for more than twenty years ([Num. 20:25-29](#Num.20.25)). He took part with Moses in numbering the people (26:3, 4), and assisted at the inauguration of Joshua. …
A Levite of the family of Merari ([1 Chr. 23:21](#1Chr.23.21), [22](#1Chr.23.22)).

The son of Dodo the Ahohite, of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the three most eminent of David’s thirty-seven heroes ([1 Chr. 11:12](#1Chr.11.12)) who broke through the Philistine host and brought him water from the well of Bethlehem ([2 Sam. 23:9](#2Sam.23.9), [16](#2Sam.23.16)).

An inhabitant of Kirjath-jearim who was “sanctified” to take charge of the ark, although not allowed to touch it, while it remained in the house of his father Abinadab ([1 Sam. 7:1](#1Sam.7.1), [2](#1Sam.7.2); comp. [Num. 3:31](#Num.3.31); [4:15](#Num.4.15)).
A son of Phinehas associated with the priests in taking charge of the sacred vessels brought back to Jerusalem after the Exile ([Ezra 8:33](#Ezra.8.33)).

A warrior of the time of David famed for his exploits. In the Authorized Version ([2 Sam. 21:19](#2Sam.21.19)) it is recorded that “Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, a Bethlehemite, slew the brother of Goliath.” The Revised Version here rightly omits the words “the brother of.” They were introduced in the Authorized Version to bring this passage into agreement with [1 Chr. 20:5](#1Chr.20.5), where it is said that he “slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath.” Goliath the Gittite was killed by David ([1 Sam. 17](#1Sam.17)). The exploit of Elhanan took place late in David’s reign.
The son of Dodo, and one of David’s warriors ([2 Sam. 23:24](#2Sam.23.24)).

Ascent, the high priest when the ark was at Shiloh ([1 Sam. 1:3](#1Sam.1.3), [9](#1Sam.1.9)). He was the first of the line of Ithamar, Aaron’s fourth son ([1 Chr. 24:3](#1Chr.24.3); comp. [2 Sam. 8:17](#2Sam.8.17)), who held that office. The office remained in his family till the time of Abiathar ([1 Kings 2:26](#1Kgs.2.26), [27](#1Kgs.2.27)), whom Solomon deposed, and appointed Zadok, of the family of Eleazar, in his stead (35). He acted also as a civil judge in Israel after the death of Samson ([1 Sam. 4:18](#1Sam.4.18)), and judged Israel for forty years.
A son of Helon, and chief of the tribe of Zebulun at the time of the census in the wilderness ([Num. 1:9](#Num.1.9); [2:7](#Num.2.7)).
One of the Gadite heroes who joined David in his stronghold in the wilderness ([1 Chr. 12:9](#1Chr.12.9)).
One of David’s sons born after his establishment in Jerusalem ([2 Sam. 5:16](#2Sam.5.16)).
A mighty man of war, a Benjamite ([2 Chr. 17:17](#2Chr.17.17)).
An Aramite of Zobah, captain of a marauding band that troubled Solomon ([1 Kings 11:23](#1Kgs.11.23)).

The son of Hilkiah, who was sent to receive the message of the invading Assyrians and report it to Isaiah ([2 Kings 18:18](#2Kgs.18.18); [19:2](#2Kgs.19.2); [Isa. 36:3](#Isa.36.3); [37:2](#Isa.37.2)). In his office as governor of the palace of Hezekiah he succeeded Shebna ([Isa. 22:15-25](#Isa.22.15)). He was a good man ([Isa. 22:20](#Isa.22.20); [2 Kings 18:37](#2Kgs.18.37)), and had a splendid and honourable career.
The son of Abiud, of the posterity of Zerubbabel ([Matt. 1:13](#Matt.1.13)).
The son of Melea ([Luke 3:30](#Luke.3.30)), and probably grandson of Nathan.
